extracted.intended_audience: educated British public / politically engaged readers (late-18th-century audience)
extracted.subtask_description: A pamphlet/essay examining principles of government, representation, and the dangers of radical revolution (Edmund Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France); argues for cautious, experience-grounded constitutional reform and against metaphysical claims of absolute rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation as basis of legitimacy (criticised)
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine (ascribed to Dr. Price and the Revolution Society) that 'a representation in the legislature of a kingdom is ... the basis of all constitutional liberty' and that without such representation a government is 'nothing but an usurpation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay presents this as the Revolutionists' central claim and then interrogates its consequences — e.g., if representation is the sole basis of legitimacy then the House of Lords and the Crown are 'bastardized' and 'no representative of the people at all'; Burke argues this principle, taken to its logical extreme, would render many established institutions illegitimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights of men must be limited by civil convention
rubrics_metrics.description: While men have natural advantages (to live, to the fruits of industry, to instruction, etc.), the share of power, authority, and direction in the state 'I must deny to be amongst the direct original rights of man in civil society; for I have in my contemplation the civil social man.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke insists civil society is 'the offspring of convention' and that rights within it are defined and limited by the conventions (laws and institutions) that create and sustain society; absolute metaphysical claims must be refracted by practical civil arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: No man should be judge in his own cause
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the first motives and fundamental rules of civil society is that 'no man should be judge in his own cause.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle requires individuals to cede certain personal prerogatives to impartial institutions; it underpins the need for conventions, impartial judiciary, and the rule of law in a functioning civil society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government as contrivance to provide for human wants
rubrics_metrics.description: Government is 'a contrivance of human wisdom to provide for human wants' rather than the mere implementer of abstract natural rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus design of government should be pragmatic and aimed at providing for practical needs (restraint on passions, distribution of resources, remedies for distempers), not purely metaphysical speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraints on men are among their rights
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to liberties, 'the restraints on men, as well as their liberties, are to be reckoned among their rights.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke argues that some restrictions are necessary for society (to bridle passions and secure justice) and these restrictions themselves are part of the rights framework that government must balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution: do not pull down established constitutions lightly
rubrics_metrics.description: It is 'with infinite caution that any man ought to venture upon pulling down an edifice, which has answered in any tolerable degree for ages the common purposes of society, or on building it up again, without having models and patterns of approved utility before his eyes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional reform should be grounded in extensive practical experience and comparative models; sudden revolutionary dismantling is warned against because the science of government is experimental and requires long experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer complex balanced institutions to simple systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple governments are 'fundamentally defective' because society's needs are complex; 'it is better that the whole should be imperfectly and anomalously answered, than that ... some parts might be totally neglected' by over-focusing on a single end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitution-makers should design multifaceted institutions and checks rather than pursue alluringly simple contrivances that excel at one purpose but fail others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights in government are compromises and middle positions
rubrics_metrics.description: The rights of men 'are in a sort of middle, incapable of definition, but not impossible to be discerned' and often require compromises 'between differences of good; in compromises sometimes between good and evil, and sometimes between evil and evil.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political judgment should compute moral trade-offs ('political reason is a computing principle') rather than insist on absolute formulas; this frames constitution-making as practical arithmetic of goods and harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish power from moral right
rubrics_metrics.description: By the theorists 'the right of the people is almost always sophistically confounded with their power' — possession of power does not automatically confer moral right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay emphasizes prudence: 'Men have no right to what is not reasonable, and to what is not for their benefit'; mere capacity to act (power) must be evaluated against reason and public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject metaphysical absolutism about 'rights of man'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Revolutionists' 'rights of men' are portrayed as absolutes admitting 'no temperament, and no compromise' and therefore as dangerous to prescription, agreement, and long-standing institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke warns that such absolutes undermine stability and make governments insecure; principles must be adaptable to circumstances and subject to prescription and compromise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical expertise and experience over metaphysical theorizing
rubrics_metrics.description: When deliberating about provisioning (e.g., food, medicine, public administration) Burke advises to 'call in the aid of the farmer ... rather than the professor of metaphysics.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those who design or reform political institutions should prioritize practical knowledge and tested experience rather than abstract political metaphysics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condemn habitual revolutionary rhetoric and sermonizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Continual talk of 'resistance and revolution' makes society 'dangerously valetudinary' — regular use of extreme remedies (revolution) weakens the spirit needed for great occasions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public discourse (sermons, societies) that treats revolution as an everyday remedy erodes moral sentiments, fosters hypocrisy, and risks producing actual violent convulsions; public leaders should avoid romanticizing revolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means of political change must be justifiable and not corrupt institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Burke lists dubious revolutionary means — seducing the army from discipline by 'debauchery' and donatives, bribing classes (e.g., citizens fed at expense of others), 'a compulsory paper currency', selling church lands to new bodies — as practices that would subvert the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures used to effect change (paper currency, bribery, dismantling tribunals, creating competing armies) are to be scrutinized and condemned if they undermine justice, discipline, and the common good; ends do not justify such destructive means.
